<reason>In a high-level exchange where both sides engaged the core development economics directly, Side A won by proving that Side B's transition mechanism creates an unworkable balance-of-payments and capital-allocation trap. Side B made a compelling case that importing essentials like fuel, food, and fertilizer drains foreign exchange, and proposed using existing mines as a bridge while directing every new loan, road, and megawatt to regional manufacturing. However, Side A dismantled this mechanism in the second half of the debate by showing that extraction is a depleting, capital-intensive sector that shrinks if starved of continuous upgrades, and that factories still require ongoing hard-currency imports (machinery, chemical precursors, spare parts) while earning local currencies from neighbors. Side A also answered Side B's pressure questions with precision—showing how tying extraction licenses to foreign-financed, dual-use power and rail locks commodity booms into physical infrastructure, and catching Side B retreating from high-value batteries to basic cement and cooking oil that cannot finance continental power grids.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In Turn 8 ([A4.2]-[A4.4]), Side A neutralized Side B's technology-shift question by noting that a specialized battery plant becomes scrap metal if battery chemistry changes whereas copper, gas, and dual-use power grids remain adaptable, and then exposed Side B's strategic retreat from batteries to local-currency cement and cooking oil while assuming depleting mines can keep earning dollars without new capital upgrades.</best_rebuttal>
